blocks.text: The qualifying-paper **short essay (200–250 words)** tests clear, correct expression on a given topic in **descriptive, analytical or reflective** mode. Unlike the Mains essay, brevity and correctness matter most — a tight **intro–body–conclusion** in a few paragraphs.

rows: 1-2 sentences framing the topic + a thesis.
2-3 short paragraphs, one idea each, with an example.
1-2 sentences summing up / a forward look.
Simple, correct, varied sentences; avoid errors.

items: Spend a minute outlining 2-3 points before writing.
Keep paragraphs short; use linking words for flow.
Prioritise **grammatical correctness** — it is a qualifying paper.
Stay within the word limit; conclude crisply.

mainsAngles: Practise 200-250-word essays across descriptive, analytical and reflective modes.
Focus on error-free, simple, well-linked prose within the word limit.

glossary.definition: The central point of the essay stated in the introduction.
Connectives (however, therefore, moreover) that give the essay flow.

blocks.text: A **formal (official/business) letter** follows a fixed format and a **polite, precise, purposeful tone**. It is used for applications, complaints, requests and official correspondence — accuracy of format and clarity of purpose are marked.

rows: 3 paras — purpose, details, request/action; polite & concise.

items: Follow the **exact format**; keep it formal and impersonal.
State the **purpose in the first line** of the body.
'Yours faithfully' with 'Sir/Madam'; 'Yours sincerely' if the name is used.
Be **concise, courteous and error-free**.

mainsAngles: Memorise the formal-letter format (addresses, subject, salutation, 3-para body, closing).
Practise application, complaint and request letters concisely and politely.

glossary.definition: A one-line statement of the letter's purpose placed before the salutation.
The formal closing used with 'Sir/Madam' when the recipient's name is not used.

blocks.text: A **press release** communicates official information to the media, while an **appeal** urges public action. Both need a **clear headline, factual body and formal source attribution** — written in an objective, third-person, information-first style.

rows: Concise, informative title of the news.
Most important info first (who, what, when, where, why, how).
A statement from the issuing authority (optional).
Persuasive but dignified; clear call to action.

items: Use the **inverted-pyramid** structure — key facts first.
Keep it **objective and third-person** (press release); persuasive yet measured (appeal).
Cover the **5 Ws and H**; end with source attribution.
For an appeal, state a clear, actionable request.

mainsAngles: Practise press releases using the inverted-pyramid (5W-1H) structure.
Write appeals with a dignified, persuasive tone and a clear call to action.

glossary.definition: A news-writing structure placing the most important information first.
The place and date of a press release, given at the start.
Who, What, When, Where, Why and How — the key questions a news item answers.

blocks.text: A **report** gives a factual, structured account of an **event, function or survey** for official record. It is written in the **past tense, third person and passive/objective voice**, with a clear title, body and conclusion.

rows: Names the event/subject of the report.
Sequence of events / findings, in logical order.
Past tense, third person, objective, factual.

items: Write in the **past tense, third person, objective** voice.
Lead with **what/when/where/who**; keep chronological or thematic order.
For a **survey report**, present findings clearly (with figures if given).
End with an outcome or recommendation; stay factual.

mainsAngles: Practise event/function reports in past-tense, third-person objective style.
Write survey reports that present findings and recommendations clearly.

glossary.definition: The line naming the reporter/author of a report.
Impersonal, factual writing without personal opinion, used in reports.

blocks.text: This task requires **describing and interpreting data** given in a graph, table or chart in prose — identifying **trends, comparisons and key figures** objectively, without adding outside information.

rows: State what the visual shows (title, variables, units, period).
Overall pattern — rise, fall, fluctuation, peak, trough.
Cite specific figures to back statements.
Summarise the main insight; no personal opinion.

items: **Read axes, units and legend first**; note the time period.
Describe **trends and comparisons**, quoting key figures.
Stay **objective** — describe only what the data shows.
Organise logically: overview → details → key insight.

mainsAngles: Practise converting graphs/tables/charts into clear descriptive prose.
Focus on trends, comparisons and data support, staying objective.

glossary.definition: The overall direction of data over time (rising, falling, fluctuating).
Citing specific figures from a visual to back a statement.

blocks.text: A **formal speech** is written to be **spoken to an audience** — it needs a courteous **address, an engaging opening, a structured body and a rousing close**, in a persuasive, audience-aware tone.

rows: 2-3 clear points with examples; logical flow; rhetorical devices.
Memorable ending — a call to action, quote or vision; thanks.

items: Open with a **greeting and a hook**; name the occasion/topic.
Use **direct address and rhetorical devices** (questions, repetition).
Keep points few and clear; **end memorably** and thank the audience.
Write for the **ear** — shorter, rhythmic sentences.

mainsAngles: Practise formal speeches with address, hook, structured body and rousing close.
Use audience-aware, persuasive language and end with a call to action.

glossary.definition: The courteous opening address to dignitaries and the audience.
A technique (question, repetition, contrast) to persuade and engage listeners.
